items.description:
### Summary

When Tornado reads an HTTP/1.1 body that uses chunked transfer encoding, it processes all chunks that have already arrived without yielding to the event loop. items.description:
### Summary

`tornado.web.RedirectHandler` builds its target URL by substituting parts of the request path into a template. Depending on where those substitutions appear in the template, an attacker can craft a request that redirects to a host of their choosing. items.description:
### Summary

Tornado's HTTP header parser takes quadratic time (O(n²)) when a header value is continued across many "obsolete line folding" (obs-fold) lines. An unauthenticated attacker can send a request whose header block is mostly short continuation lines. Parsing it uses a large amount of CPU on the IOLoop thread and blocks every other connection that process is serving.

This issue is closely related to CVE-2025-67725 (GHSA-c98p-7wgm-6p64). The fix for that advisory covered repeated headers but not line-folded continuations.

All Tornado HTTP servers are affected. Header parsing runs before any application code, so no authentication or particular handler is required.

`@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend` matches URL-type locations against `catalog.rules` location patterns using the raw URL string submitted by the user, while URL readers resolve that same string in canonical form when fetching the location's content. items.description:
### Summary

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` used two node fields without checking them.

- An array node's element list was not checked to be an array. A small payload could set the length the decoder looped over. This part is also tracked in GHSA-wp97-x4hv-qvhp.
- A sequence node's done index was not checked. A crafted value produced an iterator that never finished.

### Impact

A service that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` or `fromCrossJSON` can be made unavailable by an unauthenticated request.

- The array case blocks the thread while the decoder runs.
- The sequence case makes any code that reads the resulting iterator to the end run forever.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`.

- Element lists must be arrays.
- A sequence node's throw and done indices must be integers from -1 up to the last element index.

Invalid input throws `SerovalMalformedNodeError`.

Python Social Auth: OpenID Connect nonce is not bound to the browser session, so a stolen authorization code logs the attacker in as the victim
items.description:
### Summary

The generic OpenID Connect backend (`OpenIdConnectAuth` and every backend built on it) stores the `nonce` in the shared Association table, not in the user's session. When the ID token comes back, `validate_claims` only checks that the nonce exists in that table and is not expired. It does not check that the nonce was issued to the browser that is finishing the login.

So the nonce does not do its job. OIDC Core (section 15.5.2) and RFC 9700 (section 4.5) use the nonce to stop authorization code injection: an attacker who gets hold of a victim's unused authorization code should not be able to redeem it in the attacker's own browser. items.description:
## Summary

ONNX ConvTranspose shape inference performed an out-of-bounds read when the weight tensor had fewer than three dimensions and the model did not provide a `kernel_shape` attribute.

The inference function derived an empty `effective_kernel_shape` vector from the undersized weight tensor, then indexed that vector once for each spatial dimension of the input tensor. A crafted model passed `onnx.checker.check_model()` and caused SIGSEGV when passed to `onnx.shape_inference.infer_shapes()`.

For an input shape such as `[1, 1, 5]`, shape inference computes one spatial input dimension. A weight shape such as `[1, 3]` has no spatial dimensions, so deriving `kernel_shape` from dimensions 2 onward produces an empty vector. The output loop nevertheless accesses `effective_kernel_shape[0]`.

ONNX's Python tensor-materialization helpers could allocate memory according to attacker-controlled tensor dimensions without verifying that a packed sub-byte payload contained the declared number of elements.

A very small model could therefore cause a disproportionately large allocation when an application called `onnx.numpy_helper.to_array()` or constructed `onnx.reference.ReferenceEvaluator` with the model. The vulnerable `_unpack_2bit()` and `_unpack_4bit()` paths first allocated a small array based on the available packed bytes, then resized it to the shape declared in `TensorProto.dims`. They did not first confirm that the payload encoded enough logical elements for that shape.

ONNX shape inference did not safely validate the required Scan `num_scan_inputs` attribute. Two malformed values could terminate or disrupt the process:

1. If the attribute was missing, `ctx.getAttribute("num_scan_inputs")` returned null and was dereferenced.

### Summary
vLLM renders chat templates by passing the resolved Jinja2 source to `tokenizer.apply_chat_template()`, which compiles and `.render()`s it in an `ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment`. items.title: Wasmtime: Cranelift backend on aarch64 can jump to incorrect target on large Wasm `br_table` instruction
items.description:
## Summary

When running with the Cranelift compiler backend on an aarch64 target, Wasmtime can compile a Wasm module with more than ~256k targets on one `br_table` instruction in a way that results in an incorrect conditional branch target. This conditional branch could then jump to arbitrary other code (at an user-controlled offset), leading to arbitrary sandbox escapes.

## Impact

Any Wasmtime engine running on aarch64 with default settings can be forced to jump to arbitrary code by a user-controlled Wasm module. All versions of Wasmtime/Cranelift that support aarch64, since the initial release of that support in 2020 (before Wasmtime v1.0), are affected.

## Patches

Wasmtime v36.0.19, v48.0.7, and v49.0.4 have been released which all fix this issue.

Arbitrary file read from server filesystem via percent-encoded path traversal.

## Summary

`JaegerPropagator.extract()` in `opentelemetry-propagator-jaeger` did not enforce limits when extracting inbound `uberctx-*` baggage headers. Attacker-controlled baggage could cause unnecessary CPU work and short-lived heap allocations while processing more data than the propagator should accept.

Services that enable the optional Jaeger propagator and accept untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request resource usage. This can contribute to denial-of-service risk when transport-level limits are absent or configured above the baggage limits.

items.description:
### Summary
In affected versions, the SDK's Streamable HTTP and SSE client transports followed HTTP redirects to any host. If the configured MCP endpoint answered with a redirect to a different origin:

- custom headers set on the client (for example an `X-API-Key` credential) were sent to that origin, and
- on a `307` or `308` redirect the request body was re-sent there too.

The SDK's OAuth client providers followed redirects on their own discovery, registration and token requests in the same way.

A lone `Authorization` bearer header was not exposed; the HTTP library already drops it on cross-origin redirects.
